title: Choosing efficient mental and written calculation methods

beats.say: Open like a teacher: there is never only one way to calculate; today we learn to LOOK first and then pick. No questions.

lines.say: Here's something your teacher wants you to know. For almost any sum there are lots of ways to get the answer. A clever mathematician doesn't just pick one at random. They look at the numbers first.
The best method is called the efficient one. That means quick, simple, and not likely to go wrong.

beats.say: Mental methods suit numbers that are close, small or friendly; written methods suit big numbers with lots of exchanging. No questions.

lines.text: MENTAL: numbers that are small, close together, or next to a ten
lines.say: Mental methods, in your head, are best when the numbers are friendly: small numbers, numbers close together, or numbers sitting next to a multiple of ten.

lines.text: WRITTEN: big numbers, lots of carrying or exchanging
lines.say: Written methods are best when numbers are big and there are lots of carrying or exchanging steps, because writing keeps track for you.

beats.say: Walk through three sums and choose a method for each: 63 + 9 (near a multiple of ten -> add 10, take 1), 83 - 79 (close -> find the difference, 4), 368 + 247 (big -> written partition, 615). No questions.

lines.say: Three sums on the board. Let's choose a method for each one, and I'll tell you why.
First one. Nine is just next to a ten, so add ten and take one back: seventy-three, then seventy-two. In your head, in seconds.
Second one. Eighty-three and seventy-nine are close together, so count up the gap: seventy-nine to eighty is one, eighty to eighty-three is three. Four.
The third has big numbers, and the ones will make more than ten. That one I'd partition on paper: three hundred plus two hundred, sixty plus forty, eight plus seven.
Five hundred, a hundred, and fifteen, which is six hundred and fifteen.

beats.say: A friend uses the same long written method every time, even for 83 - 79. Show it is slow and slip-prone. No questions.

lines.say: A friend of mine always uses the long written method, even for eighty-three minus seventy-nine. They set it up in columns, then exchange a ten, then cross things out.

lines.text: They got 14. The exchange went wrong.
lines.say: And on the way they slipped, and got fourteen. That's a long way from the gap of four we found in our heads.

lines.text: A long method on an easy sum = more chances to slip
lines.say: The long method isn't wrong, but it's more work than the sum needs, and more steps means more chances to make a mistake.

beats.say: A short checklist to choose: close together? next to a ten? small number? otherwise written. No questions.

lines.text: 1. Are the numbers close?  →  find the difference
lines.say: So here's a little checklist. One: are the two numbers close together? Then find the gap.

lines.text: 2. Is one next to a multiple of 10?  →  round, then fix
lines.say: Two: is one number next to a multiple of ten, like nine, eleven, nineteen? Then round and fix.

lines.text: 3. Is it small and friendly?  →  count on or back
lines.say: Three: is the number small and friendly? Then count on or back.

lines.text: 4. Otherwise  →  partition or use columns on paper
lines.say: Four, if none of those fit: use a written method and partition.

beats.say: Always check the answer with an estimate. No questions.

lines.say: Whatever method you use, do a quick check. Three hundred and sixty-eight is nearly four hundred, and two hundred and forty-seven is nearly two fifty. Together about six hundred and fifty. Our six hundred and fifteen is close enough to make sense.

beats.say: Do two TOGETHER: 54 + 19 and 702 - 698. Choose a method for each. Operands in the intro line.

lines.say: Now you help me choose. Fifty-four plus nineteen, and seven hundred and two minus six hundred and ninety-eight.
Nineteen is next to twenty.

ask.prompt: Which method is best for 54 + 19, and what is the answer?
ask.lookFor: 73 (add 20, then take 1 back: round and fix).
ask.onMiss: Ask: is 19 close to a multiple of ten? Which one?

lines.say: Those two are very close together.

ask.prompt: And 702 − 698: which method is best, and what is the answer?
ask.lookFor: 4 (find the difference: 698 to 700 is 2, then 2 more).
ask.onMiss: Ask: are the two numbers close together? How far is 698 from 702?

beats.say: The child works alone: 456 + 378 (written), 91 - 88 (difference), and explains how they chose. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Pick the best method for each one. Four hundred and fifty-six plus three hundred and seventy-eight, and ninety-one minus eighty-eight.
Big numbers, with exchanging, so a written method.

ask.prompt: Work out 456 + 378. Which method did you pick?
ask.onMiss: Ask: add the hundreds, the tens, and the ones separately. What do you get?

lines.say: And those are close together.

ask.prompt: Work out 91 − 88. Which method did you pick?
ask.onMiss: Ask: are 91 and 88 close together? How far apart are they?

lines.text: Look at the numbers first, then choose the quickest safe method
lines.say: The big idea.

ask.prompt: In your own words: how do you decide which method to use?
ask.lookFor: Look at the numbers: close, next to a ten, or small means a mental method; big with exchanging means written.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what did you notice about 91 and 88 that made it easy?
